DC-01.reason: Randomized trials in two papers show herbicide raised native cover in most sites/cohorts, with null results only in the 1996-seeded plots.

DC-02.reason: Randomized studies disagree by species and metric: black spruce, white spruce and jack pine (one study) grew more with fertilizer, but jack pine/tamarack (another study) and first-season height showed no effect.

DC-03.reason: Several independent randomized studies show scarified plots produced taller conifer seedlings than unscarified controls, with one null height-increment contrast; the double- vs single-pass edge compares intensities, not scarification vs none.

DC-04.reason: Quasi-experimental/longitudinal evidence shows rewetting reduced tree cover/biomass and ericaceous shrub cover (the 'prevents decreased dominance' encoding contradicts its sentence, which describes reversal of canopy closure), though shrub biomass may rebound over time.

DC-05.reason: Two independent randomized experiments across multiple sites consistently show liming raised soil pH versus unlimed controls.

DC-06.reason: Liming increased sugar maple growth and white spruce height at one site, but had no effect on beech, overall height growth, or spruce at most sites.

DC-07.reason: In one quasi-experimental study rewetting raised the water table in most transects toward intact-bog levels, but not (or even deeper) in the distant T23N transect.

DC-08.reason: A single grazed-vs-ungrazed marsh comparison (associational) found lower litter mass and standing crop under grazing.

DC-09.reason: Grass-specific herbicide lowered exotic grass abundance relative to other disturbance treatments, but only at one of the sites studied.

DC-10.reason: Burn treatments (combined with other actions such as glyphosate) reduced cover of several non-native species in one study, but burning is confounded with herbicide and often compared to other treatments.

DC-11.reason: Before-after comparisons found mostly no significant change in metal concentrations in crabs and sediment, with small decreases in Cu/Hg in sediment and year-specific differences in crab Hg/Zn.

DC-12.reason: Randomized experiments in two papers found one-time mulching did not significantly change native seedling density; the 'increase' edge's sentence actually concerns exotic species changes.

DC-13.reason: Exclosure comparisons and browsing-intensity data associate moose browsing with higher foliar phenols in most sites (with exceptions); the tannin edge is not supported by its sentence, which only mentions phenols.

DC-14.reason: A randomized study found weed removal increased seedling diameter and some biomass components, though effects were site- and component-specific.

DC-15.reason: Removing weeds increased seedling diameter and biomass, implying competing vegetation reduces conifer seedling growth (site-specific, single randomized study).

DC-16.reason: Unsheltered red oak were heavily browsed, implying shelters reduce browsing damage, but the sentence reports a species contrast among unprotected trees rather than a direct shelter comparison.

DC-17.reason: Saplings inside moose exclosures were taller than outside (single observational exclosure study).

DC-18.reason: A randomized study found exponentially fertilized seedlings had greater height, diameter and biomass than conventionally fertilized ones (relative to another treatment, not untreated).

DC-19.reason: Mulch had only a borderline (p=0.06) effect on species assemblages on one date, so no clear effect is shown.

DC-20.reason: A cross-sectional chronosequence found exchangeable K stayed relatively stable after forest conversion to fallow.

DC-21.reason: Movement models show bears moving toward, away from, or indifferent to seismic lines depending on sex, season, landcover and vegetation height.

DC-22.reason: A randomized liming experiment found base saturation 1.4-3.3 times higher in limed soils than controls at both depths.

DC-23.reason: Liming increased sugar maple basal area and biomass growth but had no effect on American beech or overall height growth.

DC-29.reason: The only edge describes fertilization moderating the scarification effect, not fertilization's direct effect on diameter.

DC-30.reason: In a randomized cutting trial, total basal area was highest in the uncut control and lower in all cutting treatments (encoding says 'variation', the sentence shows reductions); stock-quality/sawlog edges are about subsets, not basal area.

DC-31.reason: Interaction results show scarification (esp. raking) reduced conifer seedling density under some cuttings but increased birch, other hardwood and non-commercial seedling density after 15 years.
